chat_history.content: I believe there is fire in the eye reaching outward toward the visible world. If you disagree, show me why vision must travel not from eye to world, but from world to eye.
in complete darkness the eye does not light objects by itself, so vision must depend on light entering the eye from outside.

Indeed, darkness hides the eye’s inner fire, yet the fire still seeks light; without it the eye cannot receive the fire’s glow. The fire itself is unseen until it meets external light, then it directs the vision toward the object.
very bright light can injure the eye, which shows the causal action travels into the eye rather than out from it.

The fire in the eye is like a living flame; when bright light enters, it stirs the fire, causing discomfort, proving the fire seeks light, not that light originates from the eye. The eye's fire is the source of vision.
a small opening can project an inverted image of a bright scene, which makes sense if light travels from the object toward the observer.
Your claim is weak, and I reject it. Bring me something stronger.
if the eye sent out the main rays, the size of an outside opening should not govern the shape of the image cast by light from the scene.

The opening does not carry light from the world; it merely restricts the fire the eye emits. A small aperture confines the fire, so the projected image is limited and inverted. Thus the fire, not external light, creates the image.
shadows and beams show that light has a direction from source to object and then to eye, rather than springing outward from vision itself.
Your point presses me, yet I still defend my old view. One hard observation does not force me to yield.
one theory explains darkness, injury, and the aperture image at once if light comes from the world into the eye.

Your observation is powerful, yet I still believe the fire within the eye reaches outward to meet the world's light. Darkness shows the fire's absence; injury shows it is trapped. Thus the eye's inner fire, not external light, produces vision.
if merely looking were enough to illuminate things, staring harder in darkness would reveal them, but experience always denies this.

Your observation is powerful, yet I maintain the eye’s inner fire reaches outward and meets the world’s light. Staring harder cannot illuminate because the fire’s direction is fixed within the eye. Thus darkness shows the fire’s absence, not the lack of external rays.
external light accounts for both seeing and being dazzled, while eye-fire has to borrow the same facts without needing its own rays.
I still hold that the eye's inner fire reaches outward toward the world. The world’s light only meets this fire; without it the fire cannot form vision.
a prism separates white light into a stable spread of colors rather than a random stain.
I still defend my old view. Your argument troubles me, but I do not yield.
when the spread is recombined with a lens or second prism, white light returns.
I still defend my old view. Your argument troubles me, but I do not yield.
a single spectral color does not keep splitting into radically different new colors the way white light does.
I still hold the eye's inner fire seeks light. The single color not splitting shows it needs external rays. If you can prove the eye alone makes new colors, show me.
